correctness.rationale: For real norm-one f,g set u=|f|, v=|g|, e=integral (u-v)_+=integral (v-u)_+, and D=integral sign(fg)min(u,v). The exact scalar formulas imply max(||f+g||_1,||f-g||_1)=1+e+|D|. Since |integral sign(fg)u-D|<=e, every g gives >=1+d(f) and simultaneously ||g-sign(fg)f||_1=2e<=2eta and |integral sign(fg)u|<=eta. The finite weighted measure u dmu has at most countably many positive atoms with summable masses, whose signed subsums form a compact set; the diffuse mass can be partitioned at every fractional value. Thus a minimizing signed bipartition exists and g=sign_A f attains R=1+d. The signed-discrepancy functional d is 1-Lipschitz in the L1 norm, so dist(f,E)>=d; normalized rescaling of the two optimal partition pieces yields h in E at distance d for d<1. When d=1, f is supported on a single atom, and dimension>=2 supplies a disjoint unit w so h=(f+w)/2 is exact and at distance one. Balanced-sign partner classification, sharp factors 2 and 1 via disjoint unit supports, and rational normalized integer PARTITION NP-completeness are verified with correct boundary cases. Independent exact rational code checked 356 profiles, 65,704 norm-one partner pairs and 356 exact sign/nearest-E witnesses. These are finite corroboration, NOT proof of the universal theorem.

value.rationale: The local almost-square infimum and exact-square locus are natural pointwise Banach-space geometry objects. The claimed theorem supplies an attained full profile for all real L1 vectors, including mixed atomic/diffuse spaces and countably many atoms, and identifies the SAME exact mass imbalance as metric distance to that locus, with sharp stable near-partner control. This is more than a textbook scalar identity or an arbitrary slice: it supplies explicit nearest-point constructions and a sharp qualitative/quantitative classification linking Banach geometry, measure splittings and combinatorial PARTITION on finite-dimensional input. The finite rational recognition problem is naturally motivated though classical PARTITION NP-completeness itself is not claimed new. A researcher studying L1 local geometry could directly use the precise local formula, the distance law and the atomic/diffuse obstruction.
